They used to make a lot of the vaults that cover a coffin out of concrete. They have a silicone type sealant that goes between the flat base of concrete on the bottom and the three sided box of concrete that sits over the top. They weigh a few hundred pounds each and in principle sound nice.

However, they don't usually work as one would hope. For instance, when a grave is dug, the concrete base must be first lowered down for the coffin to sit on. They are too heavy to lift back out even with equipment, without digging a much larger area out around them. Most of the time they get lined up and where they end up is where they end up. (Better not drop a phone underneath or it goes to the grave with whoever is going in the hole). The top is lowered on once everyone leaves the funeral.

Usually dirt will fall onto the platform and prevent a perfect seal. The lid is also very difficult to get placed 100% and will often have gaps between the two surfaces depending on how well the base was placed and top paired up.

Around here water lines are buried at 37" and literally right along side of several graves as they criss-cross the cemetery. As was pointed out earlier, in some places the water table is so low, people literally have to be entombed above ground. In New Orleans after Katrina, the gases and air trapped underground in coffins caused them to pop out of the ground. Now-a-days a lot of cemeteries have changed over to a different kind of vault. They are made out of plastic like giant Rubbermaid containers.

They still have a flat base and rounded top for covering the coffin but are much safer to handle and much less expensive. Plus they can be stacked in large quantities vs. concrete which often get poured onsite in molds. They come with sealant as well (if the cemetery isn't lazy and actually uses it). They are said to last and hold up but honestly vaults are the least of the worries with burials.

As for the Metallic objects, none of those got into the remains that we're processed. All implants are removed prior to the remains being blended. If not any metal can damage the titanium blade.

What blades?

After a body has been processed in a retort the remains are swept out of a smaller door at the rear. Some newer retorts have a drop tray but the process would be similar. Basically the remains get swept out into a collection pan for further processing.

The remains at that stage will be a mixture of ash, bone fragments and whatever physical objects that survived the burn. (Slag from teeth, medical objects, metal buttons from clothing etc...)

When examining the remains a person may see a small portion of skull or a partial femur and usually some rib fragments etc... The surviving remains are very brittle from the burn process and usually break down with minimal force at that stage. (Think a piece of wood charcoal from a campfire).

The goal for a cremation is ensure those pieces are all as uniform and unidentifiable as possible. (IE: no one wants to dump out mom or dad and have their teeth or rib fly out with some ash). The remains are placed on a cooling table designed for further processing.

They cool completely before handling and are sifted through by hand and gloves for any physical objects. Once the easily seen objects have been removed, there is a magnet that is used to sift through the remains for things like staples and smaller metal buttons etc...

In the center of the table is a big lid, resembles a soup pot lid with a rubber gasket inside the lid. Once sifting and cooling is complete, the lid is removed. Under the lid is a large steal pot with a titanium bar or blade in the bottom. The entire table sits around a motor that the pot secures to with some metal latches (It's basically a blender but with stronger motor etc).

All remains are sifted into the pot, removing anything else that might have made it by undetected before. The finer dust and ash is swept into the pot with a brush like a paint brush that is dedicated for that job. The lid is put back in and the timer started which starts the unit. (The timer is like one of those used at a hotel for the heat lamp in the bathroom).

It will run for anywhere up to 5min typically. There is a filter and fan at the top of the table that filters any dust particles from the air and the gasket on the lid is designed to help prevent dust from escaping as well. The titanium blade will break down all of the remains into a uniform consistency and make any specific things like teeth unrecognizable.

When the unit is done processing, the cremationist returns to process the remains for the final step. The latches holding the pot on the drive are removed. The table lid lifts up allowing for removal of the pot. The remains are then carefully funneled into a plastic bag that will be sealed usually with a zip tie with the bodies indentification tag attached to it. (That tag followed the body from the time they came in to the time they left to ensure no mix up or remains etc...)

The bag sits inside of a plastic box or urn. That box will be given to the funeral home and the funeral will normally transfer the bagged remains into another urn if someone bought a different kind.

Capacity depends a lot on where the crematorium is based and how many retorts they operate as well as the size of their cold storage for holding bodies.

Where we live it's pretty rural but we handle bodies from an area basically 2 hours north of us and 4 hours south of us. (Probably around 300-400 miles distance basically).

We are able to hold 3 bodies in the cooler at any given time and we operate a single retort. The turnaround is basically 3 bodies a day if you start early and go until the cemetery is locked up for the evening. It basically takes 3.5 hours average to burn and another 2-3 hours to cool the retort enough that you don't feel like your burning yourself when pushing them out of the unit. (After about 2hrs the retort will be around 800°F and at 3 hours it will still be around 650°F). Some places in larger cities may operate 3 units and have much larger storage capacity.

Funeral homes or even some coroner offices typically have cold storage units of their own. What normally happens is the funeral home will call as soon as they get someone and schedule out a date and time to bring them by. The funeral home may have a body for a few days to a week or more before they bring them in for processing.

There is paperwork that must be completed and sign offs from the medical examiner etc... You have to have proper approval from medical and family etc... Before you can process the remains. Also, a body is typically held an additional day after final approval to ensure the medical doesn't recall and want to do an autopsy or have a second check of the remains.

At that point when we receive the remains, they get entered into our system, receive a tag and identification number that stays with them until they go back to the family or funeral home. The tag follows the body throughout the entire process and is sealed onto the bag inside the urn before it's closed up.

Bodies are generally processed in a first come first serve basis and are FIFOed (First in first out) into a body cooler at refrigeration temperatures. There are rare times when a body comes in that it will be processed sooner than another that came earlier.

That is typically during times where the individual may not be suitable for storing based on smells etc... Some bodies are not found for a long period of time or die of certain types of cancers or diseases. Those bodies typically jump que to the front and get processed pretty quickly.

Bodies are normally transported from a funeral home in the back of a minivan. Sometimes but almost never do they use a hearse. The body is always covered or clothed, never naked. They typically come in body bags except for rare times they may come from certain old age homes or something.

Some funeral homes will sell a burnable coffin that can go straight into the retort. (Not worth it, also pain in the ass, they are loaded with staples). Usually, what happens when they arrive is first we assemble a box for the body to be transferred into the retort on. The box is body length and width (one size fits all). It's put together on the corners with zip ties and one side of the box is left open. There is no lid.

The box is set empty on an electronic gurney. The body in the minivan will be strapped to another gurney. They will wheel the body out of the minivan alongside the box and the body is transferred by the shoulder and ankles or by the handles on the body bag into the box. The side is then folded up and secured and the body is ready for storage in the cooler or the retort.

The retort itself is normally in it's own building and a lot of them have strict guidelines for distances and material when constructed. Because the retort gets so hot and bodies can start grease fires if not properly placed, the retort has to be in a area that would prevent the spread of fire should something happen.

The building can get pretty warm but normally there is ventilation to help heat escape and to keep the electric panel on the unit from overheating. During the summer it can be like a mini sauna the winter can be chilly but a lot depends on how hard the retort is working.

Staffing for the cemetery varies a lot depending on regions I would imagine. I worked with some pretty down to earth people, none that were like the creepy undertaker you see in the movies. One guy I worked with was going to school to be an IT guy and needed some extra cash for that.

The supervisor is a personal friend and a cowboy. You find people from all walks of life but overall the ones that can stay are able to work on their feet in the sun for hours on end in summer or winter etc...

At a cemetery your constantly mowing, shoveling, weed whacking headstones, taking trash to the dump, lifting fallen headstones, digging graves and in some areas moving sprinklers by hand etc... The retort is just a part that goes between the other jobs.

It's not really emotionally too difficult to do most days and times. It's very relaxing and you get a lot of time to listen to music, enjoy the nature, read the headstones, etc... The hard days are funerals and balancing the job of caretaker while being supportive of the family and people.

The days where you have to cremate someone you know can be hard. You get used to seeing bodies and being around them relatively quickly but you never forget those that you processed. You carry a small part of them with you in a way, you can't really forget that type of thing.

It's not like PTSD or anything crazy but it does change you. I think it makes you appreciate certain things more.
